objective.statement: Name perfect, plagal and imperfect cadences and the chord pairs that make them.
successCriteria: I know V–I is perfect, IV–I is plagal.
I know imperfect cadences end on V: I–V, ii–V and IV–V.
I use only C, G, D and F major for cadence work.

explanation.text: A cadence is a resting place at the end of a phrase, a little like punctuation in a sentence. Some cadences feel like a full stop, others like a comma. Each uses two different chords, one after the other. In Grade 5 you work with cadences in the major keys of C, G, D and F.

Two cadences end on the tonic chord. The perfect cadence is the dominant chord followed by the tonic chord (V–I). The plagal cadence is the subdominant chord followed by the tonic chord (IV–I). Any cadence that ends on the dominant chord is an imperfect cadence. At this grade the chords before the dominant are I, ii or IV: I–V, ii–V or IV–V.

music.textAlternative: A perfect cadence in C major: chord V (G, B, D) then chord I (C, E, G).

explanation.caption: Perfect cadence in C major: V–I.

music.textAlternative: A plagal cadence in C major: chord IV (F, A, C) then chord I (C, E, G).

explanation.caption: Plagal cadence in C major: IV–I.

music.textAlternative: An imperfect cadence in C major: chord I (C, E, G) then chord V (G, B, D).

explanation.caption: Imperfect cadence in C major: I–V, ending on the dominant.

explanation.text: Perfect: V–I. Plagal: IV–I. Imperfect: anything that ends on V (I–V, ii–V or IV–V). Name the last two chords first.

provenance.notes: Original wording and passages. First Steps Grade 5 section 11 (pp. 122-124, read in the PDF): perfect V–I, plagal IV–I, imperfect cadences ending on the dominant; only I–V, ii–V and IV–V are needed; cadence keys C, G, D and F major. Cadence questions are asked only where both cadence chords are in root position, so the harmony alone settles the answer.
